name: Yoga wheel
lead: A yoga wheel is a hollow plastic ring prop used for back bends and chest, shoulder and hip stretches. The Dharma Yoga Wheel was launched in summer 2014 by Dov Vargas and Raquel Vamos, who owned a New York City yoga studio and first built a $35 website to sell the wheel they had invented [1].

People use it for posture: opening the chest and extending the upper back to counter rounded, desk-bound shoulders, which supports a more upright appearance. The founders said they expected a few dozen orders from friends and students, but sales reached up to 100 wheels a day within months and $1.3 million in revenue in the first year at $99 each, with Britney Spears and several NFL players praising it on Instagram [1].
The product spread through yoga studios and social media. Forum members on T Nation mention it occasionally in mobility and yoga work alongside lifting.

angle.text: The wheel supports spinal extension and chest-opening stretches, which people use to counter slouching. Upright posture changes how tall and broad someone looks.

paras: The wheel is a plastic ring shaped to support back bending. Launched in summer 2014, it sold for $99 and was promoted for deep back stretches [1]. A Fox News profile of the company describes its growth into upgrades, spin-off products and a yoga-teacher-training program [1].
It appears occasionally in strength-training logs on forums such as T Nation, mixed with mobility and yoga work.

card.summary: A plastic ring prop for back bends and chest stretches that people use to open up the upper back and stand more upright.
card.note: Back bends can strain the spine if pushed too far.

quick.overview:
A yoga wheel is a hollow ring you roll along your back to deepen back bends and open the chest and shoulders.

People use it to counter rounded posture.
quick.mechanism: The curved ring supports the spine through extension so the upper back and chest stretch.
quick.risks: Deep back bends can strain the back; people with spinal conditions often check with a clinician first.
